scope: Independently authored before candidate retrieval outputs; bounded English smoke, not an upstream benchmark or representative quality claim
source: CrispEmbed-owned text and relevance judgements; no external dataset text
query_prompt:
Instruct: Given a question, retrieve passages that answer the question
Query:
normalization: CLS followed by L2 normalization; preserve raw CLS separately
ranking: float64 cosine of normalized vectors, descending score then ascending document ID

queries.text: A program updates two account balances. How can it prevent a crash from committing only one of the changes?
Which ordering method can schedule prerequisite tasks and also detect a circular dependency?
Which principle explains why an object keeps moving after the push ends, when no opposing force acts?
Why can a wet surface become cooler as it dries, even below the boiling point?
How can a bat locate flying prey in complete darkness?
Which check detects whether downloaded bytes differ from the publisher's file?
What allows the immune system to respond faster when it encounters the same infection again?
Which camera adjustment admits more light without increasing the exposure duration?

documents.text: Transaction atomicity makes a group of database changes succeed or fail together. Transferring money can debit one balance and credit another in a single transaction. Recovery must not expose a committed debit without its matching credit.

Durability means that a database preserves an acknowledged commit after a crash. A write-ahead log and persistent storage help recover committed changes. Durability concerns persistence rather than grouping several operations into one indivisible transaction.

Isolation controls how concurrent database transactions observe one another. Serializable execution prevents certain anomalies between simultaneous users. It is distinct from the all-or-nothing property of an individual transaction.

A topological sort orders the vertices of a directed acyclic graph so that each prerequisite comes first. Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes vertices with zero incoming edges. If unprocessed vertices remain but none has zero incoming edges, the dependencies contain a cycle.

Dijkstra's algorithm finds minimum-cost paths from a starting vertex when edge weights are nonnegative. It repeatedly expands the unsettled vertex with the least known distance. Its purpose is shortest paths rather than ordering prerequisite tasks.

Binary search locates a target in a sorted sequence by repeatedly discarding half the remaining interval. Correct boundary updates ensure termination even when the target is absent. The algorithm does not require a dependency graph.

Inertia is the tendency of an object to retain its velocity. Newton's first law says that motion remains uniform and straight when the net external force is zero. A continuing push is not required to maintain that motion.

Friction acts between contacting surfaces and often opposes their relative motion. Sliding resistance converts mechanical energy into heat. An object slowing on a rough floor experiences an external force, so its velocity need not remain constant.

Conservation of momentum relates motion before and after an interaction. In a system with no net external impulse, total momentum stays constant. During a collision, the individual objects can change velocity while their combined momentum is preserved.

Evaporative cooling occurs when relatively energetic molecules escape from a liquid surface. The remaining liquid has lower average molecular kinetic energy. Evaporation can occur below the boiling point, which is why a wet surface may cool while drying.

A liquid boils when its vapor pressure reaches the surrounding pressure, allowing vapor bubbles to grow throughout the liquid. Lower external pressure reduces the boiling temperature. Surface evaporation does not require bulk boiling.

Condensation changes vapor into liquid. It releases latent heat to the surroundings when molecules join the liquid phase. Droplets on a cold window form through condensation rather than through evaporative cooling of the glass.

Many bats use echolocation to hunt at night. They emit ultrasonic calls and analyze returning echoes to estimate an insect's direction and distance. This active sound-sensing system can operate without visible light.

An owl can locate prey by listening for sounds the prey makes. Differences in sound arrival and intensity between its ears help indicate direction. This passive listening differs from sending calls and measuring their echoes.

Some migratory birds can use the Earth's magnetic field as a navigation cue. Magnetic orientation can complement the Sun, stars and landmarks during long journeys. A magnetic compass does not directly measure an insect's distance through returning sound.

A cryptographic file checksum such as SHA-256 summarizes the exact bytes of a file. Computing the digest after downloading and comparing it with an authentic published digest detects accidental corruption or changed content. A checksum alone does not encrypt the file.

Encryption protects the confidentiality of data by transforming it with a key. Authorized recipients can decrypt the ciphertext. Confidentiality and a comparison against a publisher's file digest address different questions.

Lossless compression represents data more compactly while allowing exact reconstruction. Decompression restores the original bytes when the archive is valid. Compression is not by itself a comparison with a separately published cryptographic digest.

Adaptive immune memory can provide a faster response to a previously encountered pathogen. Memory B cells and T cells persist after an initial response and can react upon re-exposure. Vaccination aims to establish protective immune memory without the full disease.

Innate immunity supplies rapid defenses such as physical barriers, inflammation and phagocytic cells. These mechanisms recognize broad patterns associated with danger or infection. They are distinct from the antigen-specific memory emphasized in adaptive immunity.

Antibiotics act against susceptible bacteria through mechanisms such as inhibiting cell-wall synthesis. They do not directly establish the host's antigen-specific immune memory. An antibiotic that works against bacteria is not automatically a treatment for a viral infection.

Opening a camera lens aperture increases the amount of light passing through per unit time. A lower f-number denotes a wider aperture for the same focal length. This can brighten an exposure without keeping the shutter open longer, while also affecting depth of field.

A slower shutter speed increases the time during which light reaches the camera sensor. This gathers more light but can introduce blur from movement. It changes exposure duration rather than widening the lens opening.

Increasing digital image brightness multiplies recorded pixel values after capture. It cannot add photons that the sensor did not receive. Electronic gain and later processing can also amplify noise, unlike increasing the optical light admitted by the lens.
